summary: Redwood ran an Optimize-focused demo showing prefix (KV) caching, request prefetch and batching strategies and an accompanying cost model. The customer (Cobalt Labs) is evaluating a pilot for production chat routes with mixed short/long contexts and strict 99th percentile latency targets. Key concerns: data residency/keys for KV cache, bursty traffic vs steady throughput, and trade-offs between latency SLO and cost per token. Agreed next steps: share cost spreadsheet, run pilot with sample traces, align on security docs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Lee Tran (Redwood PM), Jordan Reed (Cobalt - ML Eng), Priya Nair (Cobalt - CTO), Markus Lee (Cobalt - Platform), Tess (Cobalt PM)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time, appreciate it. We're gonna focus today on Optimize features — prefix cache and batching patterns — and walk through a cost model tuned to Cobalt's chat workload. If anything's unclear shout out.

[00:22] Jordan (Cobalt): Yep thanks Alex. Quick context: our chat routes have a mix of short queries (1-3 tokens long prompts) and long context threads about 1.2k to 3k tokens. 95% of sessions are short followups but we still need to support the occasional 3k. Our 99th pctl latency target is around 350ms.

[00:45] Samira (Redwood SE): Cool, that's perfect. I sketched a few scenarios in the spreadsheet you'll see — we can do per-route policies: aggressive prefix caching for follow-ups, and fall back to full generation on warm/long contexts. We'll demo how the KV, which is our prefix cache, handles the repeated tokens and how batching reduces per-token cost.

[01:10] Markus (Cobalt): Quick Q — when you say KV cache is that resident on the inference nodes or a separate service? Security-wise we need to know where keys and cached content live.

[01:28] Samira: Great question. In Redwood Private you'd host the control plane in your VPC. The KV cache is colocated with the serving tier by default — we persist cache entries in encrypted storage and you can opt for customer-managed KMS. For Hosted we use our managed KMS but maintain strict isolation. Sometimes the transcript tool heard this as "k v cash" in older calls, haha — transcription nitpick.

[02:02] Priya (CTO): And is the cached material considered PII? We can't cache any user messages that are sensitive.

[02:12] Lee (PM): We support selective caching rules. You can tag routes or prompt templates as non-cacheable. Also, cache TTLs can be per-key or LRU based on memory pressure.

[02:35] Tess (Cobalt PM): Show us the numbers — how much do we actually save?

[02:45] Samira: For sure. I'm going to share my screen — there's a simple model: cost_per_token_hosted = base_rate * model_multiplier. With prefix caching, repeated prefix tokens are served from memory — effectively zero inference compute for those tokens — so you pay only for the suffix tokens. Batching reduces overhead by amortizing fixed kernel setup and attention overhead across multiple requests.

[03:20] [screen share noises, brief cross talk]

[04:12] Samira: Here's an example for your workload: assume 70% of sessions are 2-turn followups where the second turn reuses a 150-token system+context prefix. With a small prefix cache hit rate of 55% we'd see token compute reduced by ~30-40% on that route. If we combine that with a batching policy that groups short requests into micro-batches (50-100ms window), the per-token price drops another 10-20% because the runtime avoids single-request kernel init.

[05:05] Jordan: That micro-batch window — does that add latency above our 99th pctl SLO? We can't have users notice lag.

[05:12] Samira: Right — it's a trade. The runtime has a latency-first policy where we cap the batch window at X ms for P0 routes. For chat followups we usually configure a 30-60ms prefetch window; for background or lower-priority routes you can go up to 150-200ms. The 99th pctl impact depends on traffic shape: when traffic is bursty you get fewer batching opportunities but prefix hits still help.

[05:50] Priya: Can you walk through how prefetch works? We have multi-turn dialogs so if a user types a short message and the next turn is likely a clarification, can you precompute KV entries?

[06:05] Samira: Yes — prefetch can be route-driven. You set rules like "if this prompt pattern appears and probability_of_followup > 0.6, prefetch the next chunk asynchronously." Prefetch runs on warm nodes and populates the KV; front-line requests then see a hot cache. Important caveat: prefetch consumes compute so you should tune for expected follow rate.

[06:35] Markus: How do you estimate follow_rate? Our data is noisy.

[06:42] Alex: We ask for token distribution traces — i.e., histograms of prompt length, session length, time-between-turns. Samira can show a sample histogram and we can map that to expected cache hit and batching opportunities.

[07:03] [soft typing sounds]

[07:20] Samira: Here's a mock: your histogram shows a heavy spike at 2-4 token replies and a long tail. Using that, our model simulates per-minute throughput and simulates cache hit for prefixes that are exactly repeated or similar. There's also an approximate-match mode where we store canonicalized prefixes and match fuzzy tokens — that increases hit rate but you must accept potential quality mismatch.

[07:58] Jordan: Wait fuzzy matching — can that change the answer quality? We need determinism for certain routes.

[08:06] Samira: It can. For deterministic routes you should stick to exact prefix keys or disable prefix caching. We'll surface quality regression alerts in Console Optimize if fuzzy matches cause score drift on your eval prompts.

[08:28] Priya: About cost models, what assumptions do you make around quantization and model variant selection? Our SAS workload would likely run a 7B quantized model to save cost but we'd want the option to fall back to 13B for complex prompts.

[08:45] Lee (PM): Our cost spreadsheet includes columns for model size, q4/8 quantization multipliers, and a fallback multiplier for case-by-case escalations. You can set routing to try a quantized model first and auto-fallback when output-confidence is low. The spreadsheet multiplies tokens by model rate and adds a overhead for fallbacks and network egress.

[09:20] Tess: Can you show an example run? We want to see a real scenario with numbers.

[09:28] Samira: Sure. Open the "Cobalt example" tab. Scenario A: baseline hosted with no caching, 3k average session size for the 5% long sessions, average tokens per request 420, price ~ $0.030/token effective. Scenario B: prefix caching + micro-batching for short follow-ups — effective price goes down to $0.018/token. Over a projected 1M monthly tokens that saves roughly $12k/month.

[10:12] Jordan: That's promising. Where do we see the 99th pctl latency numbers?

[10:20] Samira: There's a console chart — per-route latency with and without batching. See here — solid lines are mean, dotted lines are 95/99. When we cap batch window to 50ms the 99th rises by ~40ms in the synthetic test. But in production with your traffic shapes we estimate 99th stays under your 350ms target.

[11:00] [brief pause]

[11:12] Markus: Ok but operationally, during a regional outage how do fallbacks behave? We don't want cascading errors.

[11:20] Alex: Redwood supports multi-tier fallback: try local quantized model, if capacity exhausted route to a regional hosted pool, if that's gone route to a smaller model, and finally degrade to cached summaries. All policies are configurable per route.

[11:45] Priya: About security again — audit logs for cache reads? We need to be able to show every read for compliance.

[11:54] Samira: Audit logs capture cache gets and puts, with user/token identifiers. In Private you can ship logs to your SIEM. We also support redaction rules so PII isn't logged.

[12:10] Tess: Are there any billing quirks — like do you charge for prefetch that doesn't get used?

[12:18] Alex: Prefetch compute is billable. In the cost sheet we assumed a 70% utilization of prefetch jobs — we also show a pessimistic 40% utilization case so you can see risk.

[12:42] Jordan: For the pilot, we'd like to start with a small set of routes, maybe 2 chat flows and one system endpoint. What instrumentation do you need from us?

[12:52] Samira: Token histograms, sample prompts (anonymized), SLO targets per route, and a whitelist for cached/non-cached templates. If you can mark those in a CSV that's easiest.

[13:08] [murmur of agreement]

[13:20] Alex: I'm gonna flip to the technical deep dive part — Samira, can you demo a quick trace where a prefix cache hit bypasses generation?

[13:30] Samira: Yep. I'll trigger a test request.

[13:35] [typing, network sounds]

[13:48] Samira: Alright you should see a trace: request arrives -> route lookup identifies cache key -> cache hit -> token stream served from cache, no GPU kernel invoked. The trace shows 11ms wall time for a small suffix compared to 72ms for full generation.

[14:10] Jordan: Nice. And the trace metadata includes which cache key matched?

[14:16] Samira: Yes, trace links to cache key id, TTL, and size. Our traces also show when fuzzy match was used — with a confidence score.

[14:40] Markus: If we move to Private, how much extra work on our infra side? We have strict change windows.

[14:48] Alex: Private deployment requires VPC peering and some infra configs but we provide an infra-as-code helm chart for on-prem and cloud. The typical install and validation takes 2-3 weeks and we recommend a staging cluster before prod.

[15:05] Priya: Does the pilot need a full Private deployment?

[15:11] Samira: Not necessarily. We can pilot on Hosted with a VPC-like tenancy and customer-managed KMS for keys, then shift to Private for production if compliance requires it. Many customers start hosted to validate workload patterns.

[15:32] Tess: Back to batching — are there built-in monitors that tell us when batching is harming latency?

[15:38] Samira: Yes Optimize console surfaces per-route batch size distributions, average wait window, and a "latency impact" metric which flags routes where batch wait > configured threshold. You get alerts and suggested actions (reduce window, pin to latency-first, etc).

[16:00] Jordan: Any gotchas with streaming responses and caching? We use streaming for typing UX.

[16:07] Samira: For streaming we do prefix caching for the underlying decoding state, but you still stream tokens as usual. If a cache hit returns full suffix, we short-circuit and stream the cached tokens. The UX impact is usually small, but ensure your client handles chunked returns with the same event IDs.

[16:35] Alex: Quick pause for questions from Cobalt that we haven't covered — anything we missed?

[16:43] Priya: We care about cost predictability month-over-month. Does your billing show predicted spend vs actual with variance?

[16:51] Lee (PM): Console shows a projection module — it runs traffic simulations to produce a predicted spend and a confidence band. You can export a CSV for finance.

[17:08] Jordan: Regarding model fallbacks, is there a metric to measure when fallback decisions hurt quality?

[17:15] Samira: Yes, we surface "fallback frequency" and tie it to eval prompt sets. If quality drops we'll flag regressions and can auto-route those requests to a higher-fidelity model for evaluation.

[17:38] Tess: Ok timeline — we want a pilot in two weeks. Realistic?

[17:45] Alex: Yes, provided we get token histograms and a sample prompt set this week. We'll provision a small dedicated pool for the pilot and run a two-week data collection.

[18:00] Priya: Security review — we'll need SOC2 docs and details on KMS integration.

[18:06] Alex: I'll put SOC2 and the KMS integration doc in the follow-up packet.

[18:20] [murmurs]

[18:30] Samira: One more tip — consider canonicalizing templates server-side before caching so that small user-specific tokens (e.g., names) don't bust the cache. We often see big win from simple canonicalization.

[18:52] Jordan: That makes sense. We'll run a quick data-cleaning pass.

[19:00] Alex: Alright let's summarize action items. Jordan, you'll give us token histograms and sample prompts by Friday. Samira will post the pilot instructions and the test harness. I'll send the cost model spreadsheet and SOC2 docs. Cobalt will review and confirm pilot routes.

[19:22] Priya: Sounds good. Any blockers from the Redwood side?

[19:27] Alex: Nope, we're good.

[19:32] Tess: Final quick Q — on billing, if prefetch spikes unexpectedly who bears the cost?

[19:39] Alex: We typically bill prefetch compute to the customer, but the pilot agreement can include a prefetch utilization cushion or a shared risk clause; we'll propose options in the spreadsheet.

[19:55] [closing pleasantries]

[20:05] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and a proposed pilot kickoff time.

[20:12] Jordan: Thanks all.

[20:15] [call ends — note: transcription contains a few mis-heard words and generic speaker labels in places]

Notes:
- References shared: "Cobalt example" tab in cost sheet (link shared in chat), SOC2 + KMS integration doc, pilot runbook.
- Transcription artifacts: occasional 'k v cash' instead of 'KV cache', Speaker labels sometimes generic.

End of transcript.
